result: CK21 is a novel triptolide pro-drug synthesized by decorating C-19 with a C-C double bond, formulated into an emulsion. Pharmacokinetic studies in rats showed CK21 had sex-dependent half-lives (1.3 hr in males, 0.225 hr in females) and converted to triptolide with stable release (30-80 nM for 2 hours), with maximum tolerated doses of 6 mg/kg for males and 3 mg/kg for females.
evaluation: Claims C5, C52, C58-C63, C65-C66 are well-supported by synthesis characterization data (NMR, mass spectrometry, X-ray crystallography) and pharmacokinetic measurements in rats. The stable release profile is documented in Figure 1e, and MTD values are provided in source data. The chemical structure and formulation are clearly described and validated.

result: CK21 demonstrated dose- and time-dependent inhibition of AsPC-1 and Panc-1 pancreatic cancer cell proliferation in vitro at 5-100 nM over 24-72 hours, with similar IC50 values to triptolide. CK21 showed minimal toxicity to primary human fibroblasts except at concentrations ≥500 nM.
evaluation: Claims C67-C69, C7 are supported by in vitro proliferation assay data shown in Figure 1f and source data 2. The dose-response and time-course data are clearly presented with appropriate controls. The selectivity for cancer cells over normal fibroblasts is demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

result: Daily CK21 treatment at 1.25-5 mg/kg significantly inhibited subcutaneous AsPC-1 tumor growth in nude mice, with complete tumor elimination at 3 and 5 mg/kg after 28 days. No tumor relapse occurred during 6-month follow-up at these doses. Treatment at ≤3 mg/kg showed no significant weight loss or organ toxicity, while 5 mg/kg caused severe weight loss. TUNEL staining showed 5-fold increased apoptosis in tumors.
evaluation: Claims C71-C77, C9, C53 are well-supported by in vivo tumor growth data (Figure 2b-c), weight monitoring (Figure 2d), H&E staining (Figure 2e), and TUNEL staining (Figure 2f-g). The long-term follow-up data (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) confirms lack of relapse. Statistical significance is demonstrated with appropriate controls.

result: CK21 at 3 mg/kg daily significantly inhibited Panc-1 tumor growth in subcutaneous xenografts and was effective at eliminating large pancreatic tumors in orthotopic xenograft models with minimal toxicity.
evaluation: Claims C78, C54 are supported by tumor growth data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 for Panc-1 subcutaneous model and Figure 2h-j for orthotopic AsPC-1 model. The efficacy is demonstrated across multiple cell lines and tumor locations.

result: In orthotopic AsPC-1 tumors, CK21 treatment resulted in 10-15-fold reduction in bioluminescence intensity compared to controls, with no deaths in the treatment group versus 5/11 sacrifices in controls. Untreated mice developed metastatic disease while CK21-treated mice did not, though all orthotopic tumors eventually relapsed after treatment cessation, unlike subcutaneous tumors.
evaluation: Claims C81-C85 are supported by bioluminescence imaging (Figure 2h-i) and survival data (Figure 2j). The differential response between orthotopic and subcutaneous tumors is noted but not fully explained. The eventual relapse of orthotopic tumors suggests incomplete eradication despite initial response.

result: CK21 completely reduced AsPC-1 tumor size after 28 days even when treatment was initiated after tumors reached ~900 mm³, demonstrating efficacy against late-stage tumors.
evaluation: Claim C86 is supported by delayed treatment data in Figure 3a-b showing complete tumor regression despite large initial tumor burden. This demonstrates therapeutic efficacy is not limited to early-stage disease.

result: Combination therapy of CK21 (3x/week) with gemcitabine did not improve tumor inhibition compared to CK21 monotherapy. However, switching to daily CK21 monotherapy induced significant tumor regression in mice that failed initial CK21, gemcitabine, or combination therapy.
evaluation: Claims C87-C88 are supported by combination therapy data (Figure 3d) and rescue therapy data (Figure 3e). The lack of synergy with gemcitabine is clearly demonstrated, and the rescue effect of daily CK21 suggests dose/schedule optimization is critical.

result: CK21 at 25-50 nM significantly inhibited growth of patient-derived pancreatic tumor organoids (UC12-0118-8, U049MAI, U123SOK, U123M15-T) in vitro after 72 hours. U049MAI organoid-derived tumors in nude mice showed significant growth inhibition with CK21 treatment (3 mg/kg daily for 28 days).
evaluation: Claims C90-C92, C8, C55-C56 are supported by organoid proliferation data (Figure 4a) and in vivo U049MAI tumor data (Figure 4b). The efficacy across multiple patient-derived organoids strengthens clinical relevance, though only one organoid was tested in vivo.

result: Time-course transcriptomic profiling of CK21-treated organoids revealed <10 differentially expressed genes at 3 hours, increasing to ~8,000 DEGs at 12 hours, indicating progressive transcriptional changes.
evaluation: Claims C10-C11, C93, C104 are supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and Figure 5a-b. The time-course design appropriately captures early and late transcriptional responses. Duplicate samples were used for each condition.

result: CK21 treatment resulted in significant downregulation of DDIT4, MYC, XBP1, and XIAP, and upregulation of POLR2A, GADD45, and VAMP1, confirmed by RT-qPCR. Similar expression profiles were observed in vivo in orthotopic AsPC-1 tumors. DDIT4 was consistently downregulated as early as 3 hours in vitro and day 3 in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C94-C97 are supported by RT-qPCR validation (Figure 4e) and RNA-seq data (Figure 4d, g). The consistency between in vitro and in vivo findings strengthens the conclusions. However, the functional significance of these early changes remains unclear.

result: DDIT4 knockdown in Panc-1 induced only modest CK21 susceptibility, and DDIT4 overexpression in AsPC-1 did not alter CK21 response. KC and KPC mouse tumors showed strong DDIT4 alterations despite modest CK21 sensitivity, suggesting early responder genes are not essential mediators of CK21 susceptibility.
evaluation: Claims C99-C103 are supported by functional validation data (Figure 4—figure supplement 3-5). The negative results from DDIT4 manipulation appropriately rule out this gene as a predictive biomarker, demonstrating rigorous hypothesis testing.

result: CK21 treatment resulted in overall inhibition of general RNA transcription, with DEGs enriched for inhibition of cell proliferation/survival and induction of apoptosis/necrosis. Ingenuity pathway analysis predicted inhibition of RNA/DNA transcription and transactivation, consistent with TUNEL-positive staining in vivo, supporting apoptosis as the mechanism of anti-tumor activity.
evaluation: Claims C12, C105-C107, C152 are supported by IPA analysis (Figure 5c) and TUNEL staining (Figure 2f-g). The transcriptional inhibition is consistent with known triptolide mechanisms. However, the claim of 'overall inhibition' may be overstated given that some genes are upregulated.

result: CK21 treatment inhibited the NF-κB pathway, with EIF2 signaling, oxidative phosphorylation, and mitochondrial dysfunction upregulated, while NF-κB, TGF-β, and telomerase pathways were downregulated at 12 hours (and NF-κB at 9 hours). Genes encoding NF-κB regulators (CHUK, IKBKB, RELA) were downregulated. Imaging flow cytometry confirmed reduced p65 expression and nuclear translocation after 24-48 hours of CK21 treatment.
evaluation: Claims C13, C108-C110, C115-C118 are supported by IPA analysis (Figure 5d-e, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and imaging flow cytometry (Figure 6a-e). The multi-modal validation (transcriptomics + protein imaging) strengthens conclusions about NF-κB inhibition.

result: CK21 treatment increased oxidative phosphorylation and caused mitochondrial dysfunction, with significantly increased expression of genes encoding mitochondrial respiratory chain complexes. ROS production showed a trend toward increase at 8 hours and significant increase at 24 hours in AsPC-1 and Panc-1 cells.
evaluation: Claims C14-C15, C119, C121-C122 are supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 6f) and ROS assay data (Figure 6g). The temporal progression from transcriptional changes to functional ROS increase is logical. However, the mechanistic link between increased respiratory chain gene expression and dysfunction requires further clarification.

result: CK21 treatment led to increased ROS production, reduced BCL2 expression in AsPC-1, Panc-1, and U049MAI after 24 hours, and cleaved caspase-3 detection in Panc-1 and organoids (confirmed by flow cytometry for Panc-1). Cleaved caspase-3/7 was not detected in AsPC-1, suggesting involvement of other effector caspases or proteases.
evaluation: Claims C16-C17, C126, C128-C130 are supported by Western blot data (Figure 6h-i) and flow cytometry (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The differential caspase activation between cell lines is appropriately noted and suggests cell-type-specific apoptotic mechanisms.

result: CK21 treatment leads to mitochondrial-mediated tumor cell apoptosis through downregulation of the NF-κB pathway, promotion of ROS production, and mitochondrial dysfunction. This is mediated by inhibition of general transcription leading to downstream effects involving NF-κB inhibition and mitochondrial dysfunction.
evaluation: Claims C18, C57, C132, C161, C173 integrate multiple lines of evidence (transcriptomics, pathway analysis, ROS assays, apoptosis markers) to support the proposed mechanism. The mechanistic model is well-supported by converging data, though some causal relationships are inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

result: CK21 is a novel triptolide pro-drug with improved pharmacokinetics and efficacy for pancreatic tumor cell lines and patient-derived organoids, exerting anti-proliferative effects by inhibiting the NF-κB pathway and inducing mitochondrial-mediated apoptosis.
evaluation: Claims C19, C172 represent the main conclusions of the study, integrating findings from pharmacokinetics, efficacy studies, and mechanism of action. The claims are well-supported by the comprehensive data presented throughout the manuscript.

result: In immunocompetent B6.129 mice, KPC-960 tumors spontaneously rejected by day 14-17 in ~70% of cases. CK21 treatment starting day 5 or 7 did not significantly inhibit tumor regression, suggesting minimal immunosuppressive activity on established primary immune responses. Mice treated with CK21 could reject secondary tumor challenges comparably to untreated mice, and splenocytes showed comparable ex vivo tumor killing, indicating CK21 did not inhibit memory/recall responses.
evaluation: Claims C135-C137, C140-C143 are supported by tumor growth data (Figure 7b-d, g), secondary challenge data, and ex vivo killing assays (Figure 7i). The spontaneous rejection model is appropriate for assessing immunosuppression. However, the resistance of KPC-960 to CK21 in nude mice (C138) complicates interpretation.

result: KPC-960 showed limited efficacy to CK21 at 3 mg/kg/day when implanted subcutaneously into nude mice, suggesting host immunity is primarily responsible for KPC-960 tumor rejection in immunocompetent mice.
evaluation: Claims C138-C139 are supported by tumor growth data in nude mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). The differential response in immunocompetent versus immunodeficient mice supports the conclusion about immune-mediated rejection. However, this raises questions about CK21's direct anti-tumor activity in this model.

result: The stable release of triptolide from CK21 may mitigate toxicity compared to other triptolide derivatives that exhibit spike release, resulting in significantly mitigated toxicity compared to analogs like F60008.
evaluation: Claims C64, C148 are speculative (explicitly stated as hypothesis/speculation) and based on comparison with historical data from other compounds. While the stable release profile is documented, direct comparative toxicity studies with other analogs are not presented. The hypothesis is plausible but requires validation.

result: The in vivo toxicity of triptolide in mice was significantly higher than CK21.
evaluation: Claim C70 is supported by comparative toxicity data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1. This demonstrates improved safety profile of CK21 versus parent compound triptolide.

result: Similar sex differences were observed for CK21 as for triptolide, with half the dose in female rats producing similar triptolide exposure as males. Female nude mice could be dosed up to 5 mg/kg/day for 28 days with tolerable weight loss, and at 3 mg/kg/day showed potent efficacy with no obvious toxicity.
evaluation: Claims C147, C150-C151 are supported by pharmacokinetic data (Figure 1e) and toxicity/efficacy data (Figure 2c-e). The sex differences are important for clinical translation but are appropriately characterized.

result: Several mechanistic claims are speculative: increased ROS may trigger mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization; AsPC-1 apoptosis may involve other effector caspases/proteases; downregulation of XBP1/ZNF628 may mediate broad transcription inhibition; gene expression changes could reflect mRNA stability rather than transcription; CK21 may tip BCL2 family equilibrium toward permeabilization.
evaluation: Claims C123, C131, C155, C162, C169 are explicitly speculative or acknowledge alternative explanations. While plausible based on the data, these mechanistic details require additional validation. The authors appropriately identify these as hypotheses rather than established facts.

result: Background claims about pancreatic cancer epidemiology, survival rates, and standard treatments are cited from established literature.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C20-C29 are background information supported by appropriate citations to established literature (DeSantis et al., Kamisawa et al., etc.). These provide context for the study.

result: Background claims about triptolide's anti-tumor activity, mechanisms, limitations, and prior analog development are cited from established literature.
evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C30-C51 provide background on triptolide and its derivatives, supported by appropriate citations. These establish the rationale for developing CK21.

result: Various background claims about orthotopic models, organoids, NF-κB function, BCL2 family proteins, apoptosis pathways, triptolide toxicity, and prior mechanistic studies are cited from established literature.
evaluation: Claims C79-C80, C89, C113-C114, C120, C124-C125, C127, C133, C144-C146, C149, C153, C156-C159, C163-C165, C167-C168 provide background information and context, appropriately supported by citations to relevant literature.

result: Supporting observations include: DDIT4 as a prognosis marker in pancreatic tumors; IPA prediction of lymphopoiesis/leukopoiesis inhibition; upregulation of DNA damage checkpoint regulation in vivo; decreased XIAP expression; reduced BCL2 in pancreatic cancer cells; subtle differences in Bcl2/Caspase-3 activation between cell lines; and broad transcription inhibition allowing CK21 to leverage distinct vulnerabilities.
evaluation: Claims C98, C134, C111, C160, C166, C170-C171 are supporting observations that strengthen the main findings. These are appropriately documented with data or citations and contribute to the overall mechanistic understanding.

result: Intravenous administration of emulsified CK21 resulted in stable release of triptolide.
evaluation: Claim C6 is supported by pharmacokinetic data showing conversion of CK21 to triptolide with stable plasma levels. This is a key feature of the formulation.
